ACIAR Monograph 143, published by the Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research (ACIAR) in partnership with NSW Department of Primary Industries, the Cambodian Agricultural Research and Development Institute (CARDI), Murdoch University, University of Canberra, and MAFF, under ACIAR Project ASEM/2000/109. text:
This source frames pest and disease management for corn around Integrated Pest Management (IPM) -- combining several strategies rather than relying on chemical pesticides alone. Recommended cultural/preventive practices include: choosing varieties with resistance or tolerance suited to local conditions; timing planting to avoid known periods of high pest or disease pressure; field sanitation (removing and destroying crop residue and volunteer plants that can harbour pests or disease between seasons); rotating with non-host crops to break pest and disease cycles; balanced fertilization (avoiding excess nitrogen, which can increase susceptibility to some pests and diseases); appropriate plant spacing and density to reduce the humid, disease-favourable microclimate inside a dense canopy; weed control to remove alternate hosts; regular field monitoring/scouting to catch problems early; and conserving natural enemies (beneficial insects) already present in the field.

Chemical pesticides are positioned as a last resort within this approach -- to be used only once an economic threshold is reached, choosing more selective products where possible, and always following label instructions and safety precautions. The goal of IPM as described here is to keep pest and disease pressure below economically damaging levels while minimising both cost and environmental/health risk, adapted to Cambodian growing conditions.
